content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors studied the performance of protein language models (PLMs) depending on the number of model parameters, and trained one of the biggest PLM to date. The authors find that larger models perform better under certain settings, and that the distribution (diversity) of the training data influences downstream performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
* The paper is overall well written
* The comparison of general PLMs trained on UniProt/BFD with antibody-specific PLMs trained on OAS is interesting and new as far as I know

## Weaknesses
* The novelty and technical contributions are limited
    * Scaling up PLMs has been investigated before, e.g. by Hesslow et al (http://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05789) or Elnaggar (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9477085)
    * Rives (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2016239118) has reported already before that the distribution (diversity) of the training data influences downstream performance
* The evaluation needs to be strengthened by more baseline models and ablation studies
* Bigger models only improve performance on certain tasks and evaluation metrics, but perform worse in some settings

1) Please compare ProGen2 to the original ProGen (v1)  throughout the paper

2) Please also compare to simple generative models such as a PSSM and LSTM, to make more clear what the performance improvements reported in Table 1 mean relative a simple model

3) Please compare the novelty of generated sequences (Figure 1) to ProGen2 models of different size and baseline models

4) Please also evaluate the quality of generative quality quantitatively, e.g. by comparing the Rosetta energy (or AlphaFold2 confidence) of generated and natural sequences, or comparing biophysical properties  (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-26529-9, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-32007-7)

5) Table 3 and table 4: Please also compare to the baseline models that are reported in table 2

6) It is expected and has been reported before (e.g. in https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-32007-7) that increasing the sampling temperature improves the novelty and diversity of generated sequences

7) It is expected that fold-specific fine-tuning will increase the similarity of generated sequences, to sequences used for fine-tuning

8) Please show more evidence via ablation that the distribution of the training data distribution influences model performance, e.g. by comparing sequence diversity and model performance when mixing 0%, 25%, ..., 100% of BFD sequences with UniRef sequences. 

9) Please provide more evidence that bigger models generalize better to higher-order mutations by analyzing model performance depending on the distance to the parent sequence.

10) I suggest strengthening conclusions by also comparing models for few-show prediction, which is relevant for practical applications.

11) The description of p^0 and p^inf, and why p^0 != p^inf is unclear and needs to be better motivated, e.g. by examples.

12) It is  unclear why the model is named ProGen2. It is not based on an improved architecture or some other methodological novelty. Just because ProGen2-xlarge has more parameters?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is overall clearly written, while the novelty is limited (see above). Results can be reproduced if the authors open-source the data and models used for training.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend rejecting the paper since the novelty and technical contributions are limited, and conclusions need to be strengthened by more rigorous evaluation experiments.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Summary of the paper:
The authors train transformers with different sizes ranging from small (151M) to large (6.4B) parameters for protein sequences. The pretrained models are released and opened for downloaded (provided as an anonymized GitHub URL in this submission). 
To train the models, they first collected diverse datasets of proteins including the protein sequences from Uniref90, the BFD90, and the antibodies database OAS.
The authors evaluated the pretrained models in three different downstream tasks: 
Language modeling on test splits of the data created from the training sets (Test-max90, Test-max50 created by considering a held-out set of protein clusters in uniref90).
Protein generation tasks 
Zero-shot fitness prediction tasks on three sets of experimentally-measured protein landscapes: narrow, wide, and antibody-specific 
 The authors also developed and released a new library called  JAXFORMER to scale the training on TPU.

Summary of the results:
Perplexity on unobserved test splits (created from the held-out clusters in uniref90) shows that the larger the models are the better the models are with smaller perplexity on test data.
For generation tasks, the authors generated 5000 sequences from the largest models. Subsequently, their 3D structure was predicted using AlphaFold, and homolog sequences were obtained from PDB. The similarity between generated sequences and homolog natural sequences is measured and demonstrated that the generated sequences are novel concerning known sequences. The authors also fine-tune the model on the data with additional steps and observed an increase in similarity with natural sequence. Antibodies generation is also evaluated similarly.
For the zero-shot fitness prediction tasks, the performance of the ProGen models was compared against state-the-art pretrained models such as MSA-Transformers, ESM-1v, RITA-XL, EVE. The base version of the ProGen model shows significantly better results than state-of-the-art models. The ensemble of different versions of ProGen shows significant results compared to all individual models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1.  The release of large pretrained models for proteins. These models were trained with diverse set of sequences including protein and antibody sequences.
2. Interesting evaluation in three different tasks including language modeling, generation and fitness prediction.

Weaknesses:
1. Novelty is limited, training approach and model architectures are standard approaches.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is a bit long given the findings demonstrated in the paper.
Novelty is limited, the main contribution is the release of large pretrained models for proteins. These models were trained with diverse set of sequences including protein and antibody sequences. However, training approach and model architectures are standard approaches. The authors also released a library for training large models on TPU called JAXFORMER but its description in the appendix does not valuate the novelty of the work.
The source-code, pretrained models are accompanied with this submission so the reproducibility is high.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My comments:
In general, this is interesting research work. The value of the work is the release of the pretrained models with very large sizes (6.4 B) for protein sequences which were trained on diverse datasets including not only protein sequences but also antibodies.
My main concern is the novelty of this work compared to existing works. In the NLP domain, people have demonstrated that training models at the size of a few hundred billion parameters are possible. Even for proteins, models with size 15B like ESM-2 were released recently (https://github.com/facebookresearch/esm)

Since training larger Language Models with more data tends to provide better results in most benchmark datasets, the race in the research fields is now the competition of training larger models with more data using large computing resources which are only available to a restricted group of researchers. This happens not only in the natural language processing research fields but now it is a trend in modeling protein sequences as well. 

I would like to see more research effort on proposing new architectures, and self-supervised training methods that leverage the physical properties of protein sequences rather than seeing bigger language models for protein sequences. I agree that making the models larger and more powerful is very relevant and useful for pushing AI-driven applications in the domains but for a research paper at ICLR I expect more on technical contribution rather than the size of the models.

Since scaling training large models such that it is more energy-sustainable and being able to scale to larger models is a very important research topic, I would like to see more description of the JAXFORMER library that is released together with this work. A description with more technical depth is needed and highlighted to demonstrate the novelty of the work.

Regarding the experiments, I know that it is very hard to evaluate generative models. The same issue happens in this work. As it relies on the measurement of the novelty of generated sequences, in my personal opinion, this is not enough to demonstrate the significance of the work. I would like to see how the generated sequences could be used in downstream applications in biomedical fields.

For evaluating protein representation, it will be more informative if the authors perform additional experiments on the TAPE benchmarks https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08230 because most state-of-the-art protein representation work reported their results on those benchmarks. Especially, the results on contact prediction, secondary structure prediction, and homology prediction are the most interesting benchmark datasets in the 5 TAPE standard datasets.

Based on the novelty and technical depth contribution, I would not recommend this work for the ICLR conference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper investigates how large protein language models (PLMs) can be used for protein design and zero-shot fitness prediction. Models at multiple scales were trained on universal set of proteins, as well as a model on the Observed Antibody Space dataset (OAS). The authors demonstrate how sequences sampled from the model can have natural structures while differing in the sequence space. Further, they show how such models can be finetuned to generate proteins with a special kind of structure. Results on fitness prediction suggest that the models can outperform prior models. There are many case studies to support the authors claims.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

* Clean scaling study of PLMs
* Interesting idea to explore the potential of using PLMs fout-of-the-box for protein design
* code and models will be open sourced

# Weaknesses

* Lots of vague statements with fairly weak quantitative evidence. Examples:
  * While the generated sequences often fold into structures resembling those produced by nature, they frequently do so with significant sequence deviations, and may adopt novel folds in some cases.  --> Is there quantitative evidence for that or is this merely a qualitative observation?
  * These results demonstrate that the sequences generated by a finetuned model sample diversity at functional regions, while maintaining the common architecture of the training dataset.  --> This is a a single observation only a single observation.
  * In practice, generating with less restrictive sampling parameters and filtering with a universal PLM should provide the most developable set of sequences. --> Should? The results don't show a strong signal imo, but it is also hard to know what a significant shift would be here. Some baseline would be helpful.
  * Empirically, we find some suggestive evidence that larger models outperform smaller models at fitness estimation in wider landscapes.
* Clarity: Many open questions (see below)
* Presentation: The plots are hard to interpret. Another form of presenting the information might have been better at times, e.g., simply some aggregated statistics/numbers rather than curves. Plots are often overloaded and too small.
* Results are not convincing. I don't think that there is a lot of evidence that using PLMs out of the box is useful.


# Questions

* How large are the fitness datasets?
* Narrow fitness landscapes: The results deteriorate for larger models. How likely is it that the benchmarks are just noisy? Can you provide error bars at least for the smaller models?
* Section 4.2 "closer inspection of predicted structures" —> How were those selected? Handpicked? 
* "Further, despite adopting similar folds, the sequence identity between the generated and natural proteins is only 10.0%." —> This is a bit ambiguous, is that the average over all generated sequences, or just selected ones?
* A scatter plot similar to 1.A comparing sequence similarity and TMScore would be helpful to make a point about sequence similarity and how it is low. There is no quantitative justification in the paper (except the ambiguous 10% similarity statement if that really holds for all sequences).
* What is the theoretical justification of changing the temperatures? You are basically changing the distribution.
* Do I understand correctly that you have shown that just not doing the temperature trick is best? (Not sure this finding deserves so much space tbh.)
* Figure 3: Sampling with higher temp is closer to the training distribution. Could it be that this simple fact explains why the sequences sampled with that temperature are better?
* What is the Sequence ID in the plots? Why is it within 0-1?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very well written but the plots should be improved. They are hard to interpret and understand and frequently overloaded.
* It is not easy to interpret the plots. 
* Assuming I understand the plots I would find it easier to understand when putting the density on the x-axis. I actually think there should be a much better way to present the interesting information one can read from these plots. Why not just using simple histograms instead, and maybe some aggregated statistics. A description of how to interpret these plots would also help. 
* Figure 3:
  * Colors change between temperatures in A and B. They shouldn’t.
  * A&B are overloaded. Easier to use some statistics for most comparisons. 

Reproducibility:
* The authors provide lots of detail and code to reproduce their research.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper and its results are interesting but do not make a convincing case for using very lagre PLMs out of the box. Most results are hard to interpret and/or seemingly weak improvements over a baseline (when there is one). The paper feels more like a proof-of-concept and lacks quantitative support for its claims, and is thus its conclusions are very vague. I am not quite convinced from the paper that PLMs are useful out-of-the-box as claimed by the authors. Many questions remain open. The presentation of the results is hard to interpret and should be improved.
